newsitem.title: INDIA: India offers incentives for investment in roads.
newsitem.headline: India offers incentives for investment in roads.

text.p: The Indian government on Thursday announced tax and import duty concessions to promote private investment in the country's overburdened roads.
Surface Transport Minister T.G. Venkatraman announced that imports of road construction machinery would be free of duty.
He said the government would offer a more liberal income tax exemption plan to road developers, and increase the peak toll rates that investors can charge.
"We have sweetened the sector further for investors," Venkatraman told a news conference. "Nobody wants to invest in roads when they have the option of telecommunications and power."
Development of roads is critical to the centre-left government's goal of raising annual growth of gross domestic product, which expanded by 6.8 percent in 1996/97 (April-March), to eight percent.
But private investors, discouraged by cumbersome land laws and a policy vacuum, have pumped relatively little money into roads compared to power and telecommunications.
Private investment in roads has so far totalled about one billion rupees ($28 million), and a further 10 billion rupees is in the pipeline, according to government estimates.
Private firms have paid about 20 billion rupees over the past two years for telecommunications licences.

"We need $1.95 billion to just expand the national highway network from the present two-lane structure to four lanes over the next five years," Yogesh Narain, the highest ranking civil servant in the Surface Transport Ministry, told Reuters.
From 1951 to 1995, the number of vehicles grew 90 times to 27.5 million but the road network expanded only seven-fold to 2.9 million km (1.8 million miles).
The volume of freight transport by road, which handles two thirds of all goods, multiplied by more than 65 times over the 44-year period.
Passenger traffic increased to 1,500 billion km (930 billion miles) in 1995 from 23 billion km (14 billion miles) in 1951, and is expected to exceed 3,000 billion km (1,860 billion miles) by 2000.
Venkatraman announced that the government was extending the period during which road developers can claim income tax benefits to 20 years from 12.
He said that the government had exempted real estate income that is ploughed back into road development from tax, and agreed to grant town ownership rights to road developers. ($1 = 35.8 rupees)
